c.tagline: Where the South Pacific still moves at village pace.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are unmetered; agree on the fare with the driver before setting off.

emergency.note: 911 is the single number for police, fire and ambulance across Samoa.

hood_landmark.Central Apia (CBD & Beach Road): Apia Clock Tower, Beach Road, Apia

avoid.reason: Watch for stray dogs and occasional petty theft after dark, and respect village evening prayer curfews (sa) outside town.

hood_desc: The commercial and waterfront heart of Apia with markets, shops, banks and Beach Road promenade; suits first-timers who want everything walkable.
A quiet harborside peninsula with government buildings and war memorials, a short walk from downtown; suits visitors wanting calm with easy access to the action.
A laid-back beachfront strip just east of downtown with a swimming lagoon and casual eateries; suits couples and travelers wanting beach access without leaving town.
Home to Samoa's largest resort on its own peninsula plus quieter residential streets further east; suits resort-seekers, families and honeymooners.
Leafy hillside area near the Robert Louis Stevenson Museum and the Cross-Island Road; suits nature lovers and drivers who don't mind being away from downtown nightlife.
lodging: Sheraton Samoa Aggie Grey's Hotel & Bungalows

water.note: Treated and generally the most reliable supply in the country, but bottled water is still the safer default for visitors.

transit.hours: Buses run roughly 6am-6/7pm in Apia (earlier finish, ~4-5pm, in outer villages); no late-night service and no fixed timetable.
transit.note: Colorful, privately owned wooden-bodied buses depart from market terminals once full, roughly every 30 minutes to 2 hours.
transit.pay: Pay the driver in cash (Samoan Tala) as you get off; there are no cards, passes or apps. Bring small notes since drivers often cannot break large bills.

tip.r: Tipping is not part of Samoan culture; some upscale resorts add a service charge to bills instead.

food.name: Palusami (Taro Leaves in Coconut Cream)
food.desc: Young taro leaves wrapped into parcels with thick coconut cream, sometimes onion or corned beef, and baked in the umu until silky.

places.name: Fugalei Fresh Produce Market
places.note: Maketi Fou cooked-food stalls sell palusami parcels made fresh each morning.

places.name: Samoa Cultural Village
places.note: Free Tuesday-to-Thursday demonstrations cook palusami in a real umu for visitors.

places.name: Taumeasina Island Resort
places.note: Fiafia buffet nights include palusami among the traditional Samoan dishes.

food.name: Oka I'a (Coconut Marinated Raw Fish)
food.desc: Raw tuna or reef fish cured in lemon juice then folded through coconut cream with onion, cucumber and chilli; Samoa's defining dish.

places.name: Amanaki Hotel Restaurant
places.note: Owns its own fishing boats, so the raw fish and poke are as fresh as it gets.

places.name: Sails Restaurant & Bar
places.note: Colonial-era building over the lagoon; seafood and oka are the reasons to book.

places.name: Apia Fish Market
places.note: Early-morning market where oka is sold in cups beside the day's landed tuna.

food.name: Umu Feast (To'ona'i)
food.desc: Sunday feast cooked above ground on hot volcanic stones: suckling pig, taro, breadfruit, fish and palusami, all smoke-scented.

places.name: Taumeasina Island Resort
places.note: Weekly fiafia night pairs a full umu spread with Samoan song and fire dancing.

places.name: Sheraton Samoa Aggie Greys Hotel
places.note: Aggie Greys fiafia night is the island's most famous feast-and-show tradition.

places.name: Samoa Cultural Village
places.note: Village guides open the umu and share the food at the end of the demonstration.

food.name: Grilled Tuna and Masimasi
food.desc: Yellowfin tuna, mahi-mahi and reef fish landed at dawn, grilled simply with lemon and coconut and served with taro or breadfruit.

places.name: Apia Fish Market
places.note: Fishermen sell straight off the boats; nearby stalls grill the catch to order.

places.name: Amanaki Hotel Restaurant
places.note: Boat-to-table seafood; consistently rated one of Apia's best kitchens.

places.name: Paddles Restaurant
places.note: Long-running harbourfront favourite doing local fish alongside Italian dishes.

food.name: Sapasui and Fa'alifu Taro
food.desc: Samoan chop suey of glass noodles, soy and beef, served with taro or green banana simmered in salted coconut cream.

places.name: Fugalei Fresh Produce Market
places.note: Cooked-food counters at Maketi Fou plate up sapasui and taro all day, cheaply.

places.name: Savalalo Flea Market
places.note: Upstairs food hall where local families eat everyday Samoan plates.

places.name: Samoa Organic Night Market
places.note: Monthly evening market of local growers and cooks, held near the end of each month.

food.name: Panipopo (Coconut Buns)
food.desc: Soft sweet bread rolls baked sitting in sweetened coconut cream so the bases soak up a caramelised coconut sauce.

places.name: Fugalei Fresh Produce Market
places.note: Bakery stalls sell trays of warm panipopo through the morning.

places.name: Nourish Cafe
places.note: European-style cafe with a Samoan twist, good for coconut baking and coffee.

places.name: Savalalo Flea Market
places.note: Home bakers bring panipopo and koko rice to the market food stalls.

food.name: Koko Samoa
food.desc: Sun-dried Samoan cocoa beans roasted and ground to a paste, then boiled into a thick, almost gritty hot chocolate drunk at breakfast.

places.name: Fugalei Fresh Produce Market
places.note: Bundles of hand-rolled cocoa and cups of hot koko sold by village growers.

places.name: Nourish Cafe
places.note: Serves koko Samoa alongside its local-produce breakfasts and smoothies.

places.name: Samoa Organic Night Market
places.note: Organic growers sell koko Samoa and cocoa products at the monthly market.

food.name: Vailima Beer and Fresh Niu
food.desc: Vailima, the national lager brewed in Apia, plus niu, a green drinking coconut hacked open and drunk cold straight from the shell.

places.name: Sails Restaurant & Bar
places.note: Breezy upstairs bar over the lagoon, the classic spot for a sunset Vailima.

places.name: Paddles Restaurant
places.note: Reliable harbourfront bar and kitchen popular with locals and expats alike.

places.name: Fugalei Fresh Produce Market
places.note: Icy drinking coconuts sold by the pile while you shop the produce aisles.

landmarks: Vailima (Robert Louis Stevenson Museum)
The restored colonial mansion where author Robert Louis Stevenson lived and died, now a museum showcasing his furniture, manuscripts, and Samoan legacy.
Mount Vaea and Robert Louis Stevenson's Tomb
A steep rainforest trail leads to the hilltop grave of 'Tusitala,' rewarding hikers with a breathtaking view over Apia and the Pacific Ocean.
Immaculate Conception Cathedral
A striking blue-and-white cathedral dominating Apia's waterfront skyline, rebuilt after cyclone damage and beloved for its vivid facade against the harbor.
Apia Clock Tower
A memorial clock tower honoring Samoans who died in World War I, standing as a central meeting point and landmark in downtown Apia.
Papase'ea Sliding Rocks
Natural volcanic rock chutes worn smooth by a freshwater stream let visitors slide straight into a cool jungle swimming pool just outside the city.
Palolo Deep Marine Reserve
A vivid coral-filled lagoon reachable by a short swim from Apia's shoreline, teeming with tropical fish and popular for snorkeling right off the capital.
Piula Cave Pool
A crystal-clear freshwater cave pool beside a historic theological college, where an underground tunnel connects to the open ocean just meters away.
Mulinu'u Peninsula
The ceremonial and political heart of Samoa, this waterfront peninsula holds government buildings, war memorials, and the tomb of past Samoan leaders.
Apia Fish and Produce Market (Maketi Fou)
A lively, colorful market hall where locals sell fresh fish, tropical fruit, and handicrafts, offering visitors an immersive taste of daily Samoan life.
Apia Waterfront and Harbour
The palm-lined seafront promenade along Apia Harbour offers postcard views of fishing boats, ferries, and the town backed by lush green mountains.

train.note: Samoa has no railways of any kind. Getting around Upolu island and to the airport is by bus, taxi or rental car; travel to other islands is by ferry or air.

bus.note: No international buses - Samoa is an island nation. Apia's colourful wooden 'aiga' buses run from the Maketi Fou (Fugalei) and downtown markets to villages across Upolu; there is no single national coach operator, and services are informal with no fixed timetable, thinning out in the afternoon and on Sundays.

ferry.note: The international ferry (MV Lady Samoa IV) sails Apia-Pago Pago from the Matautu wharf in Apia - bring your passport; it runs only about once a week, so check the schedule at ssc.ws. The same company's domestic ferry crosses Upolu (Mulifanua) to Savai'i (Salelologa) several times daily.
